mainEntity.name: What is the this keyword in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: The this keyword in Java is a reference variable that refers to the current object — the object on which the current instance method or constructor is being invoked. It is used to: (1) Disambiguate instance variables from local variables or parameters with the same name (this.name = name). (2) Pass the current object as an argument to another method. (3) Return the current object from a method (enables method chaining). (4) Call another constructor in the same class using this() — covered in the constructors topic. this cannot be used in static methods because static methods have no associated object.

mainEntity.name: What is the super keyword in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: The super keyword in Java refers to the immediate parent class of the current class. In the context of methods and fields (not constructors), it is used to: (1) Call an overridden method of the parent class from inside the overriding method — super.methodName(). (2) Access a hidden field of the parent class when the subclass declares a field with the same name — super.fieldName. super cannot be used in static methods or in a class that has no parent (though all classes have Object as the root). super always refers to the direct parent — not grandparent or higher.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between super and this in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: this refers to the current object (the instance the method is called on). super refers to the parent class of the current class. this is used to access current object's members and avoid shadowing conflicts. super is used to access parent class members that are hidden or overridden. this can be used in any instance method; super is used in subclasses to reach up to the parent. Neither can be used in static methods. In constructors, this() calls same-class constructor and super() calls parent constructor — these are covered separately.

mainEntity.name: Can we use super keyword in a static method?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — the super keyword cannot be used in a static method. super refers to the parent class in the context of a specific object instance, and static methods have no associated instance (no 'this'). Attempting to use super in a static method causes a compile-time error: 'non-static variable super cannot be referenced from a static context'. Similarly, the this keyword also cannot be used in static methods for the same reason — both keywords require an object context.

mainEntity.name: Can super skip levels in an inheritance hierarchy?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — super always refers only to the DIRECT (immediate) parent class. It cannot skip levels to access a grandparent or higher ancestor. For example, if C extends B extends A, inside C you can use super to access B's members — but you cannot use super.super to access A's members (super.super is a compile error in Java). If you need to call A's method from C, the only way is if B's method calls super (A's version) inside it, and C calls super (B's version), which chains up.

articleHeader.title: Java super and this Keywords (Methods & Fields) — Syntax, Uses, Examples & Best Practices
articleHeader.subtitle: Everything you need to know about Java super and this keywords in the context of methods and fields — this reference disambiguation, super method calls, hidden field access, method chaining, static context rules, differences, anti-patterns, and real-world production code examples.

sections.title: What are this and super Keywords in Java?

blocks.text: In Java, this and super are two special reference keywords that are available inside instance methods and constructors. They provide a way to explicitly refer to specific objects and class members when there is ambiguity or when you need to reach beyond the current class.

this is a reference to the current object — the specific instance on which the method is being called. It resolves ambiguity between instance fields and local variables, enables passing the current object as an argument, and powers fluent method chaining. super is a reference to the parent class of the current object's class. It allows a subclass to explicitly call an overridden parent method or access a field hidden by a same-named subclass field.

blocks.title: 🔑 this and super at a Glance — Methods & Fields
blocks.text: this keyword uses: (1) this.field — disambiguate instance field from local variable. (2) this.method() — call another instance method on current object. (3) pass this as argument — send current object to another method. (4) return this — enable method chaining (fluent API). super keyword uses: (1) super.method() — call parent's overridden version of a method. (2) super.field — access parent's hidden field when subclass has same-named field. Both: cannot be used in static methods. super always refers to direct parent only — not grandparent.

sections.title: this Keyword — All Uses in Methods and Fields

blocks.text: The this keyword has four distinct uses in the context of methods and fields (excluding the constructor use this() which was covered separately). Understanding each use clearly prevents a whole class of subtle bugs.

items.title: this.field — Disambiguate Field from Local Variable
items.text: When a method parameter or local variable has the same name as an instance field, 'this.field' explicitly refers to the instance field. Without 'this', the local variable shadows the field. Most common in constructors and setters: this.name = name. Required when names clash; optional (but readable) when no clash exists.

items.title: this.method() — Call Current Object's Method
items.text: this.method() explicitly calls another instance method on the current object. The 'this.' prefix is optional when calling instance methods from within the same class — Java resolves it automatically. However, writing it explicitly makes the intent clear: 'I am calling a method of this same object.' Useful for documentation and clarity in complex classes.

items.title: Pass this as Argument
items.text: The current object can be passed as an argument to another method or constructor using 'this'. Example: eventSystem.register(this) — registers the current object as a listener. Or: someHelper.process(this) — passes current object to a helper for processing. This pattern is common in observer, listener, and callback designs.

items.title: Return this — Method Chaining (Fluent API)
items.text: Returning 'this' from a method allows the caller to chain multiple method calls on the same object in one expression: obj.setName('A').setAge(25).setEmail('a@b.com'). This is the foundation of the Builder pattern and Fluent API design. Each method does its work on the object and returns the same object reference, enabling the next call.

sections.title: this for Field Access — Resolving Shadowing

blocks.text: The most common use of this is resolving variable shadowing — when a method parameter or local variable has the same name as an instance field. Without this, the local variable takes precedence (shadows the field). this.fieldName always explicitly refers to the instance field, regardless of any local variable with the same name.

blocks.label: ThisFieldAccess.java
lines: // ─── Constructor — 'this' required to distinguish field from parameter ──
public Employee(String name, int age, double salary, String department) {
// ─── Method with local var — 'this' distinguishes field ───────────────
// 'salary' here is the PARAMETER (raise amount), not the field
// No local 'department' var — 'this.' optional but can be written for clarity
this.department = newDepartment;        // ✅ also works — more explicit
age = age;   // ❌ Assigns parameter to itself — field 'this.age' unchanged!
// e.age would show 28, not 35 — silent assignment-to-self bug

blocks.title: ⚠️ The Silent this Bug — Most Dangerous Mistake
blocks.text: Writing 'age = age' (without this) in a setter or constructor where both sides refer to the LOCAL variable — not the field — is a silent bug. No compile error, no runtime exception. The field stays at its default value. Always use 'this.field = parameter' in constructors and setters. Configure your IDE to show 'assignment has no effect' warning to catch this automatically. This is one of the most common bugs in beginner Java code.

sections.title: this for Method Calls — Calling Current Object's Methods

blocks.text: Inside an instance method, you can call other instance methods of the same object with or without the this. prefix. Java resolves unqualified method calls to the current object automatically. Writing this.methodName() explicitly makes the code more readable in complex classes — it clearly documents that the method belongs to the current object, not a local helper or static utility.

blocks.label: ThisMethodCall.java
lines: this.printSummary();    // explicit this. — clearly a method of this object

sections.title: this as Method Argument — Passing Current Object

blocks.text: The this keyword can be passed as an argument to another method or constructor, sending a reference to the current object. This pattern is common in Observer, Listener, Callback, and Delegation designs — where an object needs to register itself with another object or hand itself off for processing.

blocks.label: ThisAsArgument.java
lines: // Event listener pattern — passing 'this' to register current object
// Controller implements ClickListener and passes itself
// ✅ Passing 'this' — registering current object as the listener
// Another pattern: passing 'this' to a helper/utility class

blocks.title: ⚠️ Avoid Passing 'this' from a Constructor — this Escape
blocks.text: Passing 'this' from a constructor (this escape) is dangerous — the object is not fully constructed yet when the reference is handed out. Other code may access the object before all fields are initialized, leading to null fields or incorrect state. This is especially problematic in multi-threaded code. Rule: never pass 'this' to another object or start a thread from inside a constructor. Complete all initialization first, then register/publish the object after the constructor finishes.

sections.title: Returning this — Method Chaining and Fluent APIs

blocks.text: When an instance method returns this, it returns a reference to the current object. The caller can then immediately call another method on the returned object — chaining multiple calls in a single expression. This technique is called method chaining or fluent interface design, and it is the foundation of the Builder pattern, StringBuilder, Stream API, and many modern Java APIs.

blocks.label: MethodChaining.java
lines: return this;           // ← return this = same object

blocks.title: 💡 Java's Built-in return this — StringBuilder Example
blocks.text: Java's own StringBuilder is the most-used example of return this chaining: new StringBuilder().append('Hello').append(', ').append('World').append('!').toString(). Every append() method modifies the buffer and returns 'this' — the same StringBuilder. This is why you can chain append() calls indefinitely. The Stream API, Optional, and many Spring framework methods (MockMvcRequestBuilders, ResponseEntity) also use this pattern extensively.

sections.title: super Keyword — All Uses in Methods and Fields

blocks.text: In the context of methods and fields (excluding the constructor use super()), the super keyword has two distinct uses: calling an overridden parent method, and accessing a hidden parent field. Both are used exclusively in subclass instance methods.

items.title: super.method() — Call Parent's Overridden Method
items.text: When a subclass overrides a method, the parent's version is no longer called automatically. super.methodName() explicitly invokes the parent class's version of that overridden method from within the overriding method. Use case: the subclass wants to EXTEND (add to) the parent's behaviour rather than completely REPLACE it. The parent's logic runs first, then the subclass adds its own logic on top.

items.title: super.field — Access Parent's Hidden Field
items.text: When a subclass declares a field with the same name as a parent class field, the subclass field HIDES the parent field — both exist in memory, but the unqualified name refers to the subclass field. super.fieldName explicitly accesses the parent's version of the field. Note: field hiding is rarely used and generally considered poor practice. Method overriding is almost always preferred over field hiding.

sections.title: super for Method Calls — Invoking Overridden Parent Methods

blocks.text: super.methodName() calls the parent class's version of a method that the current class has overridden. This is used when the subclass wants to augment the parent's behaviour — adding extra logic before or after the parent's implementation — rather than replacing it entirely. Without super.method(), the parent's implementation is simply skipped.

blocks.label: SuperMethodCall.java
lines: // ✅ Extends parent behaviour — calls super.log() then adds timestamp
// ✅ Extends parent format — adds uppercase on top of trim
String trimmed = super.format(text); // parent trims first
super.log(message);   // calls TimestampLogger.log() which calls Logger.log()
// Real-world pattern: Template Method with super
// ✅ Get parent description and extend it
return super.describe() + ", specifically a " + breed + " dog";
return super.describe() + ", trained as a guide dog";
// Final: 'I am an animal, specifically a Labrador dog, trained as a guide dog'
// Output: I am an animal, specifically a Labrador dog, trained as a guide dog

blocks.title: 📌 super.method() Goes Only One Level Up
blocks.text: super.method() always calls the DIRECT parent's version — never a grandparent directly. In the AuditLogger example above: AuditLogger.log() calls super.log() which is TimestampLogger.log(). Inside TimestampLogger.log(), super.log() calls Logger.log(). This creates a natural chain where each level augments the one above it. You cannot write super.super.log() in Java — it is a compile error. The chaining happens naturally through each class calling super.method().

sections.title: super for Field Access — Accessing Hidden Parent Fields

blocks.text: When a subclass declares a field with the same name as a field in the parent class, the subclass field hides the parent field (not overrides — only methods are overridden, fields are hidden). Both fields exist in memory simultaneously — the parent's field as part of the inherited state, and the subclass's field as the new declaration. super.fieldName provides access to the parent's hidden field from within the subclass.

blocks.label: SuperFieldAccess.java
lines: // ⚠️ Hides parent's 'color' field — both exist in memory
String color = "Red";   // Subclass field — hides Shape.color
// 'sides' not hidden — only one 'sides' field (inherited from Shape)
// ─── Field hiding vs Method overriding — CRITICAL DIFFERENCE ─────────────
String type = "Child field";  // HIDES parent field
public String getType() { return "Child method"; }  // OVERRIDES parent method
System.out.println("--- Field hiding vs Method overriding ---");
Base ref = new Child();   // Parent reference, child object
// FIELD ACCESS — resolved by REFERENCE TYPE (compile-time)
System.out.println(ref.type);       // Base field ← reference is Base
// METHOD CALL — resolved by OBJECT TYPE (runtime — polymorphism)
System.out.println(ref.getType());  // Child method ← object is Child
// Key insight: fields are HIDDEN (static binding), methods are OVERRIDDEN (dynamic)

blocks.title: ⚠️ Field Hiding vs Method Overriding — A Critical Distinction
blocks.text: Fields in Java are HIDDEN (not overridden). When a parent reference points to a child object, field access uses the REFERENCE TYPE (compile-time), while method calls use the OBJECT TYPE (runtime). This means 'parentRef.fieldName' accesses the PARENT's field even when the object is a child — unlike methods where dynamic dispatch picks the child's overridden version. This is why public fields are dangerous in inheritance hierarchies — behaviour depends on reference type, not object type, which is counter-intuitive. Always use methods (getters) to expose state, never public fields in inheritable classes.
While both this and super are reference keywords available in instance context, they refer to fundamentally different targets and serve different purposes.

sections.title: this and super in Static Context — Why They Don't Work

blocks.text: Neither this nor super can be used inside a static method or a static initializer block. The reason is fundamental: static methods belong to the class, not to any specific object. When a static method executes, there is no current object — there is no this. And without a current object, there is no basis for super either.

blocks.label: StaticContext.java
lines: // this.instanceId  // ❌ COMPILE ERROR: cannot use this in static context
// super.something  // ❌ COMPILE ERROR: cannot use super in static context
this.name = name;  // ✅ this in constructor — valid
super.instanceMethod();  // ✅ super.method() in instance method — valid
System.out.println("Child name: " + this.name); // ✅ this in instance method
System.out.println(Parent.staticCount);    // ✅ Use class name for static

blocks.title: 📌 The Golden Rule — this and super Need an Object
blocks.text: Both this and super fundamentally require an object to operate on. this = 'the object this method is running on'. super = 'the parent class part of the object this method is running on'. Static methods run without any object — they are class-level operations. No object means no this, which means no super. When you need to access instance state from a static method, you must receive an explicit object reference as a parameter: myStaticMethod(ClassName obj) and then use obj.field or obj.method().
These mistakes involving this and super are consistently found in Java beginner code. Most produce subtle runtime bugs rather than compile errors — making them especially dangerous.

blocks.label: KeywordMistakes.java
lines: // ❌ MISTAKE 1: Missing 'this' in setter — silent field-not-set bug

// ❌ MISTAKE 3: Expecting super to skip to grandparent

// ❌ MISTAKE 6: Returning 'this' from void method accidentally — compile error

// ✅ Fix: change return type to Dog (or Animal) to enable chaining
return this;  // ✅ Now valid — method returns Dog

blocks.text: These anti-patterns involving this and super appear in code reviews and lead to maintenance issues, subtle bugs, or code that is difficult to understand.

items.title: Field Hiding with Same-Named Subclass Fields
items.text: Declaring a field in a subclass with the same name as a parent field creates a hidden field situation — both exist, accessing either requires care, and the behaviour when accessed via a parent reference is counter-intuitive (parent's field is used). Avoid field hiding entirely — it is almost never intentional design. Use different field names in subclasses, or consolidate the field in the parent with protected access. Method overriding is a feature; field hiding is almost always an accident.

items.title: Skipping super.method() in Critical Lifecycle Methods
items.text: In frameworks like Android (onCreate, onResume), Spring, or JUnit (setUp, tearDown), overriding lifecycle methods without calling super.method() breaks the framework's internal initialization. Rule: if you override a method from a framework base class, check whether the parent's implementation does something important. When in doubt, call super.method(). The @CallSuper annotation (in Android) documents methods where super must be called.

items.title: Excessive this. Everywhere
items.text: Writing 'this.' before every single field access and method call — even when there is no shadowing — makes code unnecessarily verbose. this.name when there is no local 'name' variable, and this.process() when calling a private method, adds noise without clarity. Use this. when it adds value: in constructors/setters (disambiguates parameter), when returning this, or when passing this as an argument. Elsewhere, let Java's automatic resolution work.

items.title: Deep Method Chaining on Mutable State
items.text: While returning this enables fluent APIs, chaining 10+ method calls on a mutable object makes error handling and debugging very difficult — if one method throws an exception mid-chain, it's hard to identify which step failed. For complex construction with many optional parameters, prefer the Builder pattern (separate builder object) over chaining methods directly on the target object. Builders are easier to validate, test, and reason about.

items.title: Using super.method() to Bypass Invariant Enforcement
items.text: Sometimes a developer uses super.method() in an inner method to 'skip' validation that the overriding method adds. Example: a child class adds validation in processPayment(), but internally calls super.processPayment() to bypass it. This breaks encapsulation and the class's contract. If internal bypass is needed, refactor the parent to have a separate protected doProcess() (template method pattern) that subclasses can call without bypassing validation.

items.title: Public Fields in Inheritable Classes
items.text: Declaring public (non-final) fields in classes designed for inheritance causes field hiding problems as soon as a subclass declares a field with the same name. Since field access is resolved by reference type (not object type), behaviour becomes unpredictable when using polymorphism. Always make fields private in inheritable classes and expose them via protected or public getter methods. Methods participate in polymorphism; fields do not.

sections.title: Java super and this Keywords Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java fresher and mid-level interviews, OCPJP certification exams, and campus placement tests covering Java OOP concepts.

items.q: Q1. What are the uses of the this keyword in Java?
items.a: The this keyword in Java has four uses in methods and fields: (1) this.field — disambiguate an instance field from a local variable or parameter with the same name (e.g., this.name = name in constructors/setters). (2) this.method() — explicitly call another instance method on the current object (optional when no ambiguity exists). (3) Pass this as argument — send the current object reference to another method or constructor. (4) Return this — enable method chaining by returning the current object from a method. Additionally, this() is used in constructors to call another constructor in the same class (covered in the constructors topic). this cannot be used in static methods.

items.q: Q2. What are the uses of the super keyword in Java?
items.a: The super keyword in Java has two uses in methods and fields: (1) super.method() — call the parent class's version of an overridden method. Used when the subclass wants to extend (not completely replace) the parent's behaviour. (2) super.field — access the parent class's field when the subclass has a field with the same name (field hiding). Additionally, super() in constructors calls the parent constructor (covered separately). super cannot be used in static methods, and always refers only to the direct parent — not grandparent.

items.q: Q3. What is the difference between this and super in Java?
items.a: this refers to the current object — the instance the method is running on. super refers to the parent class of the current class. this.field/this.method() accesses current object's members; super.field/super.method() accesses parent's hidden/overridden members. this can be returned (return this) and passed as an argument; super cannot. Both cannot be used in static methods. this() and super() in constructors are the constructor-call forms of these keywords — they must be the first statement and cannot coexist in the same constructor.

items.q: Q4. Can we use the super keyword to call a grandparent's method directly?
items.a: No — super always refers to the DIRECT parent only. You cannot write super.super.method() — this is a compile error in Java. If C extends B extends A, inside C you can call super.method() which calls B's version. If B's method calls super.method(), it calls A's version. So A's method is reachable, but only through the chain — not directly from C. The chaining is enforced by each class calling super in sequence. This design ensures each level of the hierarchy has control over what runs before it delegates upward.

items.q: Q5. Can we use the this keyword in a static method?
items.a: No — this cannot be used in a static method. this refers to the current object, but static methods belong to the class and can be called without creating any object. There is no 'current object' in a static context. Attempting to use this in a static method causes a compile error: 'non-static variable this cannot be referenced from a static context'. The same applies to super. To access instance state from a static method, receive the object as a method parameter and use it explicitly.

items.q: Q6. What is the difference between field hiding and method overriding in Java?
items.a: Method overriding: when a subclass defines a method with the same signature as a parent method. The call is resolved at RUNTIME based on the actual object type (dynamic dispatch/polymorphism). Parent reference pointing to child object calls the CHILD's method. Field hiding: when a subclass declares a field with the same name as a parent field. The access is resolved at COMPILE TIME based on the REFERENCE TYPE — not the object type. Parent reference pointing to child object accesses the PARENT's field. This is why public fields in inheritable classes are dangerous — they don't participate in polymorphism.

items.q: Q7. What is method chaining and how is 'return this' used for it?
items.a: Method chaining is a design pattern where multiple method calls are chained in a single expression: obj.methodA().methodB().methodC(). It works by having each method return the current object (return this) instead of void. The returned object reference is used to call the next method. Benefits: highly readable code — reads almost like English ('new EmailMessage.from(x).to(y).subject(z).send()'). Used by: Java's StringBuilder (append().append().toString()), Stream API, Spring's MockMvc, and the Builder pattern. The return type must match the class type (or supertype) — returning void prevents chaining.

items.q: Q8. When should you call super.method() in an overriding method?
items.a: Call super.method() when the subclass wants to EXTEND (add to) the parent's behaviour — not completely replace it. Use cases: (1) The parent method has important side effects (logging, event firing, metric recording) that must run. (2) You are overriding a framework lifecycle method (Android's onCreate, Spring's afterPropertiesSet) where the parent does critical initialization. (3) You want to augment output — like a describe() method that adds to the parent's description. Do NOT call super.method() when: you intend to completely replace the parent's behaviour. The key question: does the parent's implementation do something that should always happen regardless of the subclass?

ref.show() outputs: 20 (first line — B's x, dynamic dispatch calls B.show()), then 10 (second line — super.x = A's x). ref.x = 10 — field access through a parent reference uses the REFERENCE TYPE (A), so it returns A's x = 10 even though the object is a B. Key takeaway: method calls use runtime object type (polymorphism — B.show() runs). Field access uses compile-time reference type (no polymorphism — A.x is returned via A ref). This is the classic demonstration of method overriding vs field hiding.

items.q: Q10. What is 'this escape' and why is it dangerous?
items.a: 'This escape' (or unsafe publication of 'this') occurs when the current object reference (this) is passed out of the constructor before the object is fully constructed — e.g., passing this to another object's method, adding this to a static collection, or starting a thread with a reference to this inside a constructor. Danger: (1) The receiving code may immediately call methods on the partially constructed object — fields could be null or at default values. (2) In multi-threaded code, other threads may see the object before all fields are safely published. (3) If the class is subclassed, the subclass constructor hasn't run yet when super() is called — even more fields are uninitialized. Fix: complete all initialization in the constructor, then publish/register the object after the constructor returns — in a factory method or init() call.

items.a: Output: 'B: 10' then 'super: 5' then 'A: 5'. Explanation: new B().show() calls B's overriding show(). Inside B.show(): 'x' refers to B's field (10) → prints 'B: 10'. 'super.x' accesses A's hidden field (5) → prints 'super: 5'. 'super.show()' calls A's show() — inside A.show(), 'x' refers to A's own field (5) → prints 'A: 5'. Note: inside A.show(), there is no shadowing — A only knows its own x = 5.

Bug: 'width = width' and 'height = height' assign each parameter to itself — the instance fields are never updated (they remain at default 0.0). So area() returns 0.0 * 0.0 = 0.0, not 15.0. Fix: use 'this.width = width; this.height = height;'. The this. prefix is required here to distinguish field (this.width) from parameter (width). Without this., both sides of the assignment refer to the local parameter — a classic silent bug with no compile error.

Yes, it compiles. Output: 'Animal eating' then 'Dog eating'. new Dog().action() → action() calls this.eat() — since object is a Dog, this.eat() calls Dog's eat(). Inside Dog.eat(): super.eat() calls Animal.eat() → prints 'Animal eating'. Then Dog.eat() continues → prints 'Dog eating'. The this.eat() call inside action() is equivalent to just eat() — the 'this.' is optional but valid. Dynamic dispatch ensures Dog's eat() runs, not Animal's.

String result = new StringBuilder().append("Hello").append(", ").append("World").append("!").toString(); System.out.println(result); — StringBuilder.append() returns 'this' (the same StringBuilder), enabling the chain. Each append() call modifies the internal buffer and returns the same StringBuilder object. toString() at the end converts the buffer to a String. This produces 'Hello, World!' — identical to the verbose version but in one expression.

Output: 'Parent' (line 1) then 'Child' (line 2). p.name — field access via Parent reference → compile-time resolution → Parent's 'name' field = 'Parent'. Fields are HIDDEN, not overridden — reference type decides which field. p.display() — method call via Parent reference with Child object → runtime resolution (dynamic dispatch) → Child's display() runs → prints 'Child'. Methods ARE overridden — object type decides which method. This output perfectly demonstrates: same reference, two different resolution mechanisms for fields vs methods.

items.q: 6. Design a fluent Person class where you can chain: new Person().name("Arjun").age(25).city("Mumbai") and then call print() to display all fields.

items.a: Output: 100 (line 1) then 200 (line 2). Line 1 — obj.value: obj is declared as Base. Field access is resolved by REFERENCE TYPE at compile time (no polymorphism). Reference is Base → Base.value = 100. Line 2 — obj.getValue(): method call is resolved by OBJECT TYPE at runtime (dynamic dispatch). Object is Derived → Derived.getValue() runs → returns this.value = Derived's value = 200. The same reference 'obj' gives different results depending on whether you access a field directly or through a method. This is why public fields in inheritable classes are dangerous — always use getter methods to ensure polymorphic behaviour.

Uses of 'this': (1) this.brand = brand — in Vehicle constructor: disambiguates field 'brand' from parameter 'brand'. (2) this.speed = speed — same, disambiguates field from parameter. (3) this.batteryKWh = batteryKWh — in ElectricCar constructor: disambiguates field from parameter. (4) return this — in setBattery(): returns current ElectricCar object, enabling method chaining. Uses of 'super': (5) super(brand, speed) — in ElectricCar constructor: calls Vehicle's parameterized constructor to initialize inherited fields. (6) super.info() — in ElectricCar.info(): calls Vehicle's overridden info() to get 'brand@speed', then appends battery info on top. Result: ElectricCar.info() returns e.g. 'Tesla@200+100kWh'.

sections.title: Conclusion — this and super: The Two Lenses of Java OOP

blocks.text: this and super are two lenses through which Java code looks at its own object hierarchy. this looks inward — at the current object, its own fields and methods. super looks upward — at the parent class, its implementation before it was overridden, its fields before they were hidden. Together they give subclasses full visibility into both their own state and their inherited state.

Mastering these keywords separates clean OOP code from buggy, confused code. The hallmarks: this.field = param in every constructor and setter, super.method() whenever extending (not replacing) parent behaviour, return this for fluent APIs, never using either in static contexts, and always preferring method overriding over field hiding.

rows: Prevent silent assignment-to-self bug in constructors/setters
Reach parent's same-named field — rare, avoid field hiding
No object context in static scope

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions — Java super and this Keywords

items.q: What is the this keyword in Java?
items.a: The this keyword is a reference to the current object — the instance the method or constructor is running on. Uses: (1) this.field to disambiguate instance field from local variable (this.name = name). (2) this.method() to explicitly call current object's method. (3) Pass this as argument to another method. (4) Return this from a method to enable method chaining. Cannot be used in static methods — no object exists in static context.

items.q: What is the super keyword in Java?
items.a: The super keyword refers to the parent class of the current class. In methods and fields (not constructors): (1) super.method() calls the parent's overridden version of a method — used to extend, not replace, parent behaviour. (2) super.field accesses the parent's field when the subclass has a same-named field (field hiding). super cannot be used in static methods and always refers to the direct parent only — not grandparent.

items.q: What is the difference between super and this in Java?
items.a: this refers to the current object; super refers to the parent class. this.field/this.method() accesses current object's members; super.field/super.method() accesses parent's hidden/overridden members. this can be returned and passed as argument; super cannot. Both are unavailable in static methods. In constructors: this() calls same-class constructor; super() calls parent constructor — both must be the first statement.

items.q: Can we use super keyword in a static method?
items.a: No — super cannot be used in a static method. super requires an object context (it refers to the parent class part of the current object). Static methods have no associated object instance. The compile error is: 'non-static variable super cannot be referenced from a static context'. The same applies to this. To access instance-level members from a static method, receive an explicit object reference as a parameter.

items.q: Can super skip levels in an inheritance hierarchy?
items.a: No — super always refers only to the DIRECT parent. You cannot write super.super.method() — it is a compile error. If C extends B extends A, from inside C: super.method() calls B's version. If B.method() calls super.method(), it calls A's version. The chain happens naturally — each level calls super, which goes one more level up. You cannot jump from C directly to A, bypassing B.
